title: "How strong is the benchmark?"
description: >
  What "an omitted variable as strong as the benchmark" means, in partial

  benchmark-strength block come from.
---

<!-- Generated from benchmark-strength.Rmd.orig by precompute/precompile.R. Edit the .orig file, not this one. -->



`bootmakr` reports the coefficient you would have obtained had a variable "as
strong as" an observed covariate been omitted. That phrase needs a
definition, and readers who are used to the impact threshold of a confounding
variable (ITCV) expect one in terms of correlations. The block that
`bootmakr` prints below its results gives it. This article explains what the
block contains, how to reproduce it, and what it should not be used for.

## Two relationships, two numbers

An omitted variable biases a regression coefficient only if it is related to
both the treatment and the outcome. `sensemakr` measures the two
relationships with partial R^2^ values (Cinelli & Hazlett, 2020):

- the share of the variance of the **treatment** that the omitted variable
  explains, after the observed covariates have explained what they can;
- the share of the variance of the **outcome** that it explains, after the
  treatment and the observed covariates have explained what they can.

The square roots of these shares are the absolute values of partial
correlations. Nothing is known about an omitted variable, so the same two
numbers are computed for an observed covariate, the benchmark, and the
omitted variable is then assumed to be a multiple of it.

## The block

We use the data of the [worked example](ceo-pay.html): the effect of a
family CEO (`owner_ceo`) on the logarithm of CEO pay, with CEO tenure as the
benchmark and two multiples of it.


``` r
library(bootmakr)
library(haven)

osf  <- "https://osf.io/download/stk7y/?view_only=885d1ed5498c4b3c8a1194882e468286"
chen <- read_dta(osf)

ceo.model <- lg_ceopay ~ owner_ceo + ceo_tenure + PA_nic3_med + ceo_edu_dummy +
  lg_sales + firm_age + promoters_pct + institutions_pct +
  factor(year) + factor(nic_code_1digit)

out <- bootmakr(ceo.model, data = chen, treat = "owner_ceo",
                benchmark_covariates = "ceo_tenure", kd = c(0.5, 1),
                cluster = "co_code", reps = 100, seed = 123, progress = FALSE)

out$benchmark_strength
#> $type
#> [1] "single"
#> 
#> $observed
#>    benchmark   r2dxj.x    r2yxj.dx   r_dxj.x  r_yxj.dx
#> 1 ceo_tenure 0.1446519 0.003425632 0.3803313 0.0585289
#> 
#> $implied
#>    benchmark  kd  ky     r2dz.x     r2yz.dx    r_dz.x    r_yz.dx
#> 1 ceo_tenure 0.5 0.5 0.08455735 0.002353248 0.2907875 0.04851029
#> 2 ceo_tenure 1.0 1.0 0.16911470 0.004836676 0.4112356 0.06954621
```



(The block does not depend on the bootstrap, so a small number of
replications is enough here.)

`$observed` describes the benchmark. CEO tenure explains
14.5 percent of the variance of family-CEO status
that the other covariates leave unexplained (`r2dxj.x`) and
0.3 percent of the variance of log CEO pay that the
treatment and the other covariates leave unexplained (`r2yxj.dx`). The
partial correlations are .38 and
.06: tenure is clearly related to who is a
family CEO and only weakly related to pay once family-CEO status and the
other controls are held fixed.

`$implied` describes the omitted variable that each row of the results table
assumes: its partial R^2^ with the treatment (`r2dz.x`) and with the outcome
(`r2yz.dx`), and the corresponding partial correlations.

In Stata the same numbers are printed below the bootstrap table and returned
in `r(r2dxj_x)`, `r(r2yxj_dx)` and the matrix `r(benchmark_strength)`.

## Where the numbers come from

The observed strength can be reproduced from two regressions: the model
itself, and a regression of the treatment on the covariates.


``` r
fit   <- lm(ceo.model, data = chen)
fit.d <- lm(update(ceo.model, owner_ceo ~ . - owner_ceo), data = chen)

# benchmark with the outcome, given the treatment and the other covariates
sensemakr::partial_r2(fit, covariates = "ceo_tenure")
#>  ceo_tenure 
#> 0.003425632

# benchmark with the treatment, given the other covariates
sensemakr::partial_r2(fit.d, covariates = "ceo_tenure")
#> ceo_tenure 
#>  0.1446519
```

A partial R^2^ of a single covariate is a function of its *t* statistic and
the residual degrees of freedom, *t*^2^ / (*t*^2^ + df), and the *t*
statistic used here is the conventional one. This does not make the block
depend on the choice of standard errors. The partial R^2^ is equally the
proportional reduction in the residual sum of squares when the covariate is
added to the model, a quantity that involves no standard error at all. The
*t* statistic is only a convenient way of computing it.


``` r
rss <- function(m) sum(residuals(m)^2)
1 - rss(fit) / rss(update(fit, . ~ . - ceo_tenure))
#> [1] 0.003425632
```

The implied strength of the omitted variable follows from the observed
strength of the benchmark. `kd` is defined as the variance of the treatment
explained by the omitted variable relative to the variance explained by the
benchmark, both measured after the *remaining* covariates have been taken
into account. Restating this as a partial R^2^ given *all* covariates,
benchmark included, gives


``` r
kd  <- c(0.5, 1)
r2d <- sensemakr::partial_r2(fit.d, covariates = "ceo_tenure")

kd * r2d / (1 - r2d)
#> [1] 0.08455735 0.16911470
```

which is the column `r2dz.x`. The corresponding value for the outcome,
`r2yz.dx`, is an upper bound that also depends on `ky` and on the benchmark's
relationship with the treatment. Cinelli and Hazlett (2020) derive both
expressions. This is why the omitted variable at `kd = 1` is somewhat
stronger than the benchmark itself in the block: the two are measured
against different sets of covariates.

`bootmakr` takes these values from `sensemakr`. You can obtain them directly:


``` r
bounds <- sensemakr::ovb_bounds(fit, treatment = "owner_ceo",
                                benchmark_covariates = "ceo_tenure",
                                kd = c(0.5, 1))
bounds[, c("bound_label", "r2dz.x", "r2yz.dx", "adjusted_estimate")]
#>       bound_label     r2dz.x     r2yz.dx adjusted_estimate
#> 1 0.5x ceo_tenure 0.08455735 0.002353248         0.2927133
#> 2   1x ceo_tenure 0.16911470 0.004836676         0.2541140
```

The last column is the adjusted estimate that `bootmakr` reports and
bootstraps.

## What the block is for

**It makes the assumption concrete.** "An omitted variable as strong as CEO
tenure" becomes "an omitted variable with partial correlations of about
.41 with family-CEO status and
.07 with CEO pay". Readers can judge
whether that is a little or a lot in their field.

**It describes the data, not the inference.** Every number in the block is a
function of the data alone. It is the same under conventional,
heteroskedasticity-robust and cluster-robust standard errors, and the same
in every bootstrap run. The problem that motivates `bootmakr`, that robust
standard errors change the *t* statistic on which the ITCV rests, does not
touch it.

**It is not a threshold.** The block does not say how strong an omitted
variable must be to overturn the result. That would require a critical value,
which brings the standard error back in. Whether a given strength overturns
the result is answered by the bootstrap confidence interval in the table
above the block, and the strength at which it first does so is the
[breakdown point](ceo-pay.html#the-breakdown-point). Note also that the
outcome correlation in the block is conditional on the treatment, whereas
the ITCV is stated in correlations that are not. The two scales are close
relatives, but a number from the block should not be compared with an ITCV
as if they were the same quantity.

## When the assumed strength is impossible

An omitted variable cannot explain more variance than there is left to
explain. If `kd` is so large that the implied partial R^2^ reaches 1,
`sensemakr` cannot compute the adjusted estimate. In a bootstrap this can
happen in some replications and not in others, because the strength of the
benchmark is re-estimated in every bootstrap sample. `bootmakr` drops such
replications and reports how many failed. A few failures are of no concern.
Many of them mean that the assumed strength is near the limit of what the
data allow, and that a smaller `kd` or a weaker benchmark is the more
informative question to ask.

Cinelli, C., & Hazlett, C. (2020). Making sense of sensitivity: Extending

82(1), 39--67. <https://doi.org/10.1111/rssb.12348>

Lonati, S., & Wulff, J. N. (2026). *Why you should not use the ITCV with
robust standard errors (and what to do instead)*. Working paper.
